summary: Defines MIME, which lets email carry multi-part messages and non-text content such as images without losing information. It is based on RFC 934 and RFC 1049, extending and revising that earlier work. It was replaced by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048, RFC 2049.

plainLanguage.summary: MIME gives email body content labels that identify its type and how it was encoded. It also defines a way to put several parts, including non-text data, in one message.

questions: what is base64 encoding in email
how does content transfer encoding work
subtitle: How MIME labels email content and encodes data for mail transport.

tldr.problem: The RFC 822 message body was flat ASCII text, which could not directly describe multiple parts, other character sets or non-text data.
tldr.mechanism: MIME adds header fields to identify a message version, the body type and any transfer encoding. It defines multipart bodies and seven top-level content types.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1521 revised RFC 1341 and was later obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049.

today: RFC 1521, a Draft Standard, obsoleted RFC 1341 and has been obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049. RFC 1590 updated it.

sections.title: Why Email Needed MIME
sections.content:
RFC 822 described message headers but left the body as flat ASCII text. That limited email to short lines of seven-bit data and did not provide a standard way to include images, audio or text in other character sets.

MIME defines body mechanisms that retain compatibility with existing message formats. It does not extend message headers beyond US-ASCII; a companion document handles that separate issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Older email formats described simple text bodies. MIME adds standard labels and structures for messages containing other kinds of content.

sections.title: Headers Describe the Body
sections.content:
MIME-Version identifies a message as following this MIME specification; a conforming message includes MIME-Version: 1.0. Content-Type names the body's type and subtype, with optional parameters such as a character set.

The seven initial top-level types are text, multipart, message, image, audio, video and application. A receiving program can use the content type to choose how to handle the body. If the field is absent, the default is plain text in US-ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: The headers tell a receiving program what kind of data the body contains. For example, Content-Type can identify text, an image or a multipart body.

sections.title: Transfer Encodings
sections.content:
Content-Transfer-Encoding identifies a reversible transformation used to carry data through a transport with limited character or line support. The defined values are 7bit, 8bit, binary, quoted-printable and base64. The first three label data forms without transforming them.

Quoted-printable can leave many printable characters readable and represent other octets with an equals sign and hexadecimal digits. Base64 encodes arbitrary octets in printable characters; its output is about 33 percent larger than the original.
sections.plainLanguage: A transfer encoding changes a body into a form that a mail transport can carry. The receiver uses the named encoding to restore the original data.

sections.title: Multipart and Message Bodies
sections.content:
The multipart type combines multiple body parts in one entity, and each part can have its own headers and body. A boundary parameter marks where parts begin and end. The RFC defines mixed, alternative, parallel and digest multipart subtypes for different relationships among parts.

The message type can contain another message. The partial subtype represents a message split across several messages, and external-body points to data stored elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: A multipart message contains separate parts, each with its own content and description. A message body can also contain another message or refer to content held elsewhere.
